title: Gears, belts and chains: ratios, torque and efficiency
goals: Work out the output speed of a gear pair, a belt drive or a chain drive
Work out the torque a gearbox gives out, allowing for its efficiency
Work out a motor's torque from its power and speed
Combine stages: multiply the ratios, multiply the efficiencies
Work out a conveyor's belt speed from the drum and the drive
summary:
Where two gears mesh, their teeth pass at the same rate. So **speed × teeth** is the same for both:

$n_2 = n_1 \frac{z_1}{z_2}$, with $z$ the teeth and $n$ the speed in rpm.

The **ratio** $i = \frac{z_2}{z_1}$: a 20-tooth pinion driving a 60-tooth wheel is 3:1, a **reduction**. Each meshing pair reverses the direction; an **idler** between them changes the direction back but not the ratio.

**Belts and chains**: the belt's speed is the same at both pulleys, so **speed × diameter** is the same: $n_2 = n_1 \frac{d_1}{d_2}$. For chains, use the sprocket teeth. V-belts slip a little (about 1–2%); toothed belts and chains do not.

**Torque**: power in is power out, less losses. A reduction slows the shaft down and raises the torque by the same ratio:

$T_2 = T_1 \times i \times \eta$

$\eta$ (eta) is the **efficiency**, as a decimal: about 0.97–0.98 for a spur or helical stage, 0.95–0.98 for a belt or chain, much less (0.5–0.9) for a worm gear.

**Several stages**: multiply the ratios, and multiply the efficiencies.

**Torque from power**: $T = \frac{9550 P}{n}$ (T in N·m, P in kW, n in rpm). A 4 kW motor at 1440 rpm gives about 26.5 N·m.

**Linear speed** of a belt on a drum (or a chain on a sprocket): $v = \frac{\pi d n}{60}$ (d in metres, n in rpm, v in m/s).

resources.title: ABC's of Gears (basic guide, PDF)
resources.note: Gear types, tooth terms and speed ratios, from a gear maker.

sources: Childs, P. R. N.: Mechanical Design Engineering Handbook, 2nd edition (Butterworth-Heinemann): gears, belts and chains
Hughes Electrical and Electronic Technology, 10th edition (Pearson): motor torque and power

formulas.name: Gear speeds
formulas.says: The teeth pass each other at the same rate, so the gear with more teeth turns more slowly, in proportion.
formulas.example: 20 teeth at 1500 rpm driving 60 teeth: $1500 \times \frac{20}{60} = 500$ rpm.

formulas.name: Pulley speeds
formulas.says: The belt moves at one speed, so the bigger pulley turns more slowly, in proportion to the diameters.
symbols: the driven pulley's diameter (same units as d₁)
formulas.example: 100 mm at 1450 rpm driving 250 mm: $1450 \times \frac{100}{250} = 580$ rpm.

formulas.name: Torque out of a reduction
formulas.says: The output torque is the input torque times the ratio, less what the gearbox loses.
symbols: the efficiency as a decimal (0.95 for 95%)

formulas.name: Torque from power and speed
formulas.says: Power is torque times speed. 9550 makes the units come out: kW and rpm in, N·m out.

formulas.name: Linear speed of a belt or chain
formulas.says: Each turn moves the belt one circumference (π times the diameter); n turns a minute is n ÷ 60 a second.
formulas.example: A 0.2 m drum at 90 rpm: $\frac{\pi \times 0.2 \times 90}{60} = 0.94$ m/s.

bench.task: On a machine that is isolated and locked off, find one belt or chain drive and work out its ratio from what you can count and measure.
check: Count the sprocket teeth, or measure both pulley diameters
Work out the ratio: big ÷ small
Read the motor's rated speed off its plate
Work out the driven shaft's speed, and compare it with the machine's documents or a tachometer reading later, with guards back on

cards.q: A 20-tooth gear on a motor drives a 60-tooth gear. Compared with the motor shaft, the output shaft turns…
options: a third as fast, with about three times the torque
three times as fast, with a third of the torque
a third as fast, with a third of the torque
at the same speed, the other way round
cards.why: The 60-tooth gear has three times the teeth, so it takes three motor turns to turn it once. Power in is (nearly) power out, so slowing it down three times raises the torque about three times.

cards.title: Gear ratio: teeth pass at the same rate
cards.body:
Where two gears mesh, every tooth on one meets a tooth on the other. So in a minute the same number of teeth go by on both:

$$n_1 z_1 = n_2 z_2 \quad\text{so}\quad n_2 = n_1 \frac{z_1}{z_2}$$

$n$ is the speed (rpm), $z$ the number of teeth; 1 is the driver, 2 the driven.

The **ratio** is $i = \frac{z_2}{z_1}$: 60 teeth driven by 20 is **3:1**, a **reduction**. Each meshing pair turns the other way.
cards.more:
Count it. A 20-tooth pinion turns once: 20 of its teeth go past the meshing point. The 60-tooth wheel moves on 20 teeth too, a third of a turn.

So the motor at 1500 rpm gives $1500 \div 3 = 500$ rpm on the wheel.

The ratio is written big over small for a reduction: 3:1 means three turns in for one out. A gearbox plate saying i = 10 or 10:1 means the output turns ten times slower than the input.

An **idler** gear between the two only passes the motion along: it reverses the direction back, and its own tooth count cancels out of the ratio.

cards.q: A {a}-tooth pinion turning at {n} rpm drives a {b}-tooth gear. How fast does the gear turn?
cards.why: Speed × teeth is the same on both gears, so the bigger gear turns slower by the ratio of the teeth. Multiplying by $\frac{{b}}{{a}}$ instead (the ratio upside down) gives a speed-up, which a small gear driving a big one cannot do.
cards.hint: Speed × teeth is equal for both gears.

cards.title: Slower means more torque
cards.body:
A gearbox cannot make power; it trades speed for **torque**. Slow the shaft down by a ratio $i$ and the torque goes up by $i$, less the losses:

$$T_2 = T_1 \times i \times \eta$$

$T$ is torque in newton-metres (N·m), $i$ the reduction ratio, $\eta$ (eta) the **efficiency** as a decimal (0.95 for 95%).

Typical efficiencies: a spur or helical stage 0.97–0.98, a belt or chain 0.95–0.98, a **worm** gear 0.5–0.9 (lower at high ratios).
cards.more:
Think of a bicycle: a low gear lets you climb a steep hill (lots of torque at the wheel) but you pedal fast for little speed. Same power from your legs, traded the other way.

Power is torque times speed. If a motor gives 20 N·m at 1500 rpm into a 10:1 box, the output turns at 150 rpm. For the power to match, the torque must be 10 times bigger: 200 N·m. Real gears lose a little to friction and oil churning, so at 95% you get $200 \times 0.95 = 190$ N·m.

The lost 5% becomes heat in the gearbox: on a 10 kW drive that is 500 W, which is why big gearboxes run warm.

cards.q: {t} N·m goes into a {r}:1 gearbox that is {e}% efficient. What torque comes out?
cards.why: Torque rises by the ratio, then the losses come off: × the efficiency as a decimal.
cards.hint: Multiply by the ratio, then by the efficiency (÷ 100 for a decimal).

cards.title: A motor's torque from its plate
cards.body:
A motor plate gives the **power** (kW) and the **speed** (rpm), not the torque. Power is torque times speed, so:

$$T = \frac{9550 P}{n}$$

$T$ in N·m, $P$ in **kW**, $n$ in **rpm**. The 9550 is just the units: 60 seconds a minute, 1000 W a kW, and $2\pi$ radians a turn ($60\,000 \div 2\pi \approx 9550$).
cards.more:
Numbers first: a 5.5 kW motor at 1450 rpm. $9550 \times 5.5 = 52\,525$, and $\div 1450 = 36.2$ N·m. That is the rated torque it can give all day.

A 5.5 kW motor at 2900 rpm (2-pole) gives half that, 18.1 N·m: same power, twice the speed, half the torque.

After a 10:1, 95% gearbox: $36.2 \times 10 \times 0.95 = 344$ N·m at 145 rpm. Check by power: $\frac{344 \times 145}{9550} = 5.2$ kW, which is the 5.5 kW less the 5% loss.

cards.q: A motor plate says {p} kW at {n} rpm. What is its rated torque?
cards.why: Torque is power ÷ speed; the 9550 takes care of kW and rpm.

cards.title: Belts and chains
cards.body:
A belt moves at one speed all the way round, so at both pulleys the rim speed is the same: **speed × diameter** is equal.

$$n_2 = n_1 \frac{d_1}{d_2}$$

$d$ is the pulley diameter. A **chain** is the same as gears: use the sprocket **teeth**.

**V-belts** grip by friction and slip a little (about 1–2%), so the speed is a touch under the sum. **Toothed (timing) belts** and chains do not slip: use them where position matters.

Unlike a gear pair, a belt or chain keeps both shafts turning **the same way**.
cards.more:
Wrap a string round a big wheel and a small one. Pull a metre of string: it goes a metre round each rim. The big wheel's circumference is longer, so it turns fewer times.

Motor pulley 100 mm, driven 250 mm: the driven turns $\frac{100}{250} = 0.4$ times for each motor turn. At 1450 rpm that is 580 rpm (about 570 rpm on a V-belt, after slip).

To speed a fan up, you fit a bigger motor pulley or a smaller fan pulley. Check the fan's power rises too: for a fan it goes up much faster than the speed (see pumps and fans).

cards.q: A motor at {n} rpm has a {d1} mm pulley driving a {d2} mm pulley on a toothed belt. How fast does the driven pulley turn?
cards.why: The belt's speed is the same at both rims, so the speeds are in the ratio of the diameters, small over big for the driven speed. A toothed belt does not slip, so this is exact.
cards.hint: Speed × diameter is the same at both pulleys.

cards.title: Stages: multiply them
cards.body:
Most drives have more than one stage: a belt into a gearbox, or a gearbox with two or three pairs of gears inside.

- The **overall ratio** is the ratios **multiplied**: 3:1 then 4:1 is 12:1.
- The **overall efficiency** is the efficiencies **multiplied**: 0.97 × 0.97 = 0.94.

A **worm gear** gives a big ratio (20:1, 50:1) in one stage, at right angles, but loses more: often 0.5 to 0.8. A worm at a high ratio can be **self-locking**: the load cannot turn it backwards.
cards.more:
Add them and you get nonsense: a 3:1 then a 4:1 is not 7:1. Follow a turn through: the first stage turns once for every 3 input turns; the second turns once for every 4 of those. That is once per 12 input turns.

Efficiencies multiply for the same reason: the second stage loses its 3% of what the first stage passed on, not of the original.

Three helical stages at 0.97: $0.97 \times 0.97 \times 0.97 = 0.91$. A single 40:1 worm might be 0.6, so for the same output torque its motor must be much bigger, and 40% of the power becomes heat in the box.

cards.q: A belt drive of {r1}:1 ({e1}% efficient) feeds a gearbox of {r2}:1 ({e2}% efficient). What is the overall efficiency, in per cent?
cards.why: Each stage passes on its own fraction of what it receives, so the fractions multiply. The ratios multiply too ({r1} × {r2}), but they do not come into the efficiency.
cards.hint: Multiply the efficiencies as decimals, then back to per cent.

cards.title: From drum speed to belt speed
cards.body:
A conveyor belt moves one drum **circumference** ($\pi d$) for every turn of its drive drum. So:

$$v = \frac{\pi d n}{60}$$

$v$ is the belt speed in m/s, $d$ the drum diameter in **metres**, $n$ the drum speed in rpm (÷ 60 for turns a second).

Work back through the drive: motor speed, ÷ the ratio for the drum speed, then this.
cards.more:
One turn of a 0.3 m drum moves the belt $\pi \times 0.3 = 0.94$ m. At 60 rpm (one turn a second) that is 0.94 m/s.

To set a conveyor speed with a drive, run it backwards: the wanted belt speed gives the drum rpm ($n = \frac{60v}{\pi d}$), times the gearbox ratio gives the motor rpm, and the motor rpm sets the drive's frequency (a 4-pole motor runs about 30 rpm per Hz).

cards.q: A conveyor's drive drum is {d} mm across and turns at {n} rpm. How fast does the belt move?
cards.why: One turn is one circumference, $\pi d$, in metres; rpm ÷ 60 is turns a second.

cards.q: A 4 kW motor runs at 1440 rpm into a 12:1 gearbox, 95% efficient. What are the output speed and torque?
cards.why: Speed comes down by the ratio; torque goes up by the ratio, less the losses. Checking the power is a quick way to catch a ratio used upside down.

cards.q: Why does step 4's power check catch mistakes?
cards.context: 302 N·m at 120 rpm works back to 3.8 kW, against a 4 kW motor.
cards.model: A gearbox cannot make power, only lose a little. So the output power must come out a few per cent below the motor's. If the ratio had been used upside down (speed multiplied instead of divided, or torque divided), the output power would come out wildly different from the motor's: many times bigger or smaller. A result close to the input, slightly less, means the speed and torque are consistent.
points: Power out cannot exceed power in
Output power should be just under input power
A ratio used upside down makes the powers far apart
It checks speed and torque together

cards.q: A 1460 rpm motor drives a 100 mm pulley, belted to a 200 mm pulley on a 15:1 gearbox. How fast does the gearbox output turn?
cards.why: Ratios multiply through the stages. (A V-belt's slip would take about 1–2% off.)

cards.q: A {p} kW motor at {n} rpm drives a {r}:1 gearbox, {e}% efficient. What torque does the output give?
cards.why: Torque from the plate first, then up by the ratio and down by the losses.
cards.hint: Motor torque from $T = \frac{9550 P}{ n }$, then × ratio × efficiency.

cards.q: A fitter works out a gearbox output. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: Motor: 2.2 kW at 1420 rpm, so $T = 9550 \times 2.2 \div 1420 = 14.8$ N·m
cards.why: A 20:1 reduction divides the speed. 28 400 rpm out of a gearbox fed at 1420 is impossible, and the power check (266 N·m at 28 400 rpm is about 790 kW from a 2.2 kW motor) shows it at once.

cards.q: A 20-tooth gear drives a 35-tooth idler, which drives a 60-tooth gear. What is the overall ratio?
options: 3:1, and the output turns the same way as the input
3:1, and the output turns the opposite way to the input
5.25:1, the same way as the input
1.75:1, the opposite way to the input
cards.why: The idler's teeth cancel: $\frac{35}{20} \times \frac{60}{35} = \frac{60}{20} = 3$. Two meshes reverse the direction twice, so the output turns the same way as the input.

cards.q: A {a}-tooth sprocket at {n} rpm drives a {b}-tooth sprocket by chain. How fast does the driven sprocket turn?
cards.why: A chain is like gears: the links pass the same number of teeth on both sprockets, so speed × teeth is equal.
cards.hint: Use the teeth, as for gears.

cards.q: A hoist uses a 40:1 worm gearbox. Why might the designer have chosen a worm over a helical box?
options: One compact stage, and it can be self-locking
Worm gears are more efficient than helical ones
A worm keeps both shafts on the same axis
Worm gears never need any lubrication
cards.why: A worm gives a big ratio in one stage at right angles, and at high ratios it can resist being driven backwards by the load. The price is efficiency: often 60% or less, where a helical stage is about 97%. (A hoist still needs a proper brake: self-locking is not a safety device.)

cards.q: A mixer needs {t} N·m at {n} rpm. It is driven through a gearbox that is {e}% efficient. What motor power does it need, in kW?
cards.why: Work the power the load needs, then divide by the efficiency: the motor must also supply what the gearbox loses. Then pick the next standard motor size up.
cards.hint: $P = \frac{Tn}{9550}$ at the output; the motor must give more, by the losses.

cards.q: A belt drive has a 150 mm motor pulley and a 300 mm driven pulley. Which changes by a factor of 2, and which way?
options: Speed halves and torque roughly doubles
Speed doubles and torque roughly halves
Speed halves and torque halves too
Speed halves; torque stays the same
cards.why: Small driving big is a 2:1 reduction: half the speed. Power is (nearly) kept, so torque about doubles. Belts and gears follow the same trade.

cards.q: A {n} rpm motor drives a {r}:1 gearbox, whose output turns a {d} mm conveyor drum. How fast does the belt move?
cards.why: Two rules in a row: the ratio for the drum speed, then circumference × turns a second for the belt.
cards.hint: Drum speed first, then $v = \frac{\pi d n}{60}$ with d in metres.

cards.q: Three gear stages, each {e}% efficient. What is the overall efficiency, in per cent?
cards.why: Efficiencies multiply, they do not add or average: three stages at {e}% is $({e}\%)^3$. Subtracting 3 × the loss is close for small losses but not exact.

cards.q: A 15-tooth gear drives a 45-tooth gear. The output turns…
options: a third as fast, with about three times the torque
three times as fast, with about a third of the torque
a third as fast, with the same torque
three times as fast, with the same torque
cards.why: 45 ÷ 15 = 3:1 reduction: a third of the speed and, power being kept, about three times the torque.

cards.q: A {p} kW motor at {n} rpm drives a {r}:1 gearbox at 95%. What torque comes out?
cards.why: Motor torque from power and speed, then × ratio × efficiency.

cards.q: A {d1} mm pulley at {n} rpm drives a {d2} mm pulley. How fast does the driven pulley turn (no slip)?
cards.why: Speed × diameter is the same at both pulleys.

cards.q: Match each drive with what it is known for.
pairs: Big ratio in one stage; can be self-locking
Quiet and forgiving, but slips a little
No slip, so it keeps position
